To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) We identified novel cellular replisome-associated protein(s) at replication forks of proliferating EBV-transformed lymphoblastoid cell lines and Burkitt lymphomas; and (2) We validated the role of these proteins in the cell cycle and survival of EBV-infected cells.
novel replisome-associated ZFPs are upregulated early in the EBV infection of B cells and are expressed at high levels by EBV-infected cells in the blood of transplant patients.

we have identified several novel cellular proteins at replication forks of proliferating EBV-transformed lymphocytes, including three zinc finger proteins, which are upregulated during EBV infection and promote survival of proliferating cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular pathogenesis of EBV-driven B lymphoproliferations and how the virus overcomes cell-intrinsic barriers that normally limit cellular DNA replication.
understanding the mechanisms of EBV-driven lymphomagenesis, and in the process we have uncovered a novel set of proteins that may play a critical role in EBV-driven lymphoma.
the role of the EBV oncogene, LMP1, in promoting cell proliferation and survival.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study has identified several cellular proteins, not previously known to be linked to DNA replication, which are upregulated in EBV-transforming B cells and Burkitt Lymphomas.
we have identified several cellular proteins at replication forks of cells transformed by the oncogenic Epstein-Barr virus.
we have identified eight novel proteins associated with replication forks of EBVs-transformed cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified several novel proteins that are present at cellular replication forks and that may be important for the survival and proliferation of EBV-transforming cells and Burkitt Lymphoma.
we have identified several proteins that are associated with replication forks in EBVs-transformed B cells and Burkitt Lymphoma cells.
we have discovered novel proteins that are associated with the replication fork of EBV-transforming B cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
EBV-infected cells have evolved to overcome cellular barriers to replication and that this process may be exploited therapeutically.
the replication machinery is a dynamic and plastic structure that can be modified in response to cellular needs.
EBV-transformed lymphoma cells have an unusual DNA replication phenotype that is distinct from that of untransformed lymphocytes.
